extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys, examiners), inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether an invention satisfies statutory and judicial requirements for patent protection (novelty, utility, subject-matter, prior use, and related defenses). Focuses on principles used by courts to determine validity and scope of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: No prior public disclosure or abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention was publicly disclosed or abandoned to the public before the patent application, the patent will be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains that public use or abandonment by the inventor before application defeats the right to a patent. Courts treat public use or sale (without inventor's consent) as potentially depriving the inventor of patent rights; the statute carves out exceptions (see two-year rule). Examples/anti-patterns: allowing free public individual use or public divulgence before filing can bar patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible prior user/purchaser defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A person entitled to claim statutory protection must be a purchaser or one who used the invention before the patent was issued by a license, grant, or with the inventor's consent — not a purchaser from a mere wrong-doer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases illustrate that purchasers or users who acquired the invention legitimately from the inventor (or under his consent) before application can continue to use it after patent issuance. A purchaser from a fraudulent pirate or with full notice/knowledge of fraud is not protected. Example: employee who made experiments in employer's manufactory, permitted use by employer, was within statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exceptions: abandonment and two-year bar
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute preserves patent validity despite prior purchase/sale/use by the inventor prior to application except where there is proof of abandonment to the public or where such prior purchase/sale/use occurred more than two years before application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets 7th section of 1839 Act: sale/use by inventor before application will not invalidate patent unless inventor abandoned the invention or the prior use was >2 years before filing. The section's clauses must be read to protect purchasers from the inventor and to limit inventor's right to file after extended pre-filing commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent or wrongful public use by others does not bar inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrongful, fraudulent, or secret use of an invention by others, or public use without the inventor's consent or knowledge, will not deprive the inventor of his right to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise stresses uniform doctrine: courts will not allow a pirate's wrongful acts to cut off the prior inventor's rights. Thus, prior use that is wrongful (done without inventor's consent) cannot create a valid defense to the inventor's later patent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute (worldwide) novelty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty under the law relates to inventions made anywhere in the world — the invention must be absolutely new, not known or used anywhere and not described in any public work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work states novelty must be absolute and not merely relative. However, later statutory caveat (see foreign prior use proviso) relaxes this where foreign uses were not patented or printed and the applicant believed himself first inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign prior use/published exception when inventor believed himself first
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee, at the time of filing, believed himself to be the first inventor, the patent is not void because of prior foreign knowledge or use unless the thing (or substantial part) had been previously patented or described in print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proviso relieves original inventors from the presumption arising from prior foreign knowledge or secret foreign use, provided there is no prior patent or printed description. The patentee's oath of believing himself first can be dispositive against mere foreign use.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as a 'public work' or 'printed publication'
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have not fully defined 'described in some public work' or 'described in any printed publication'; a workable requirement may be that the description must serve as a direction for making or doing the thing described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance suggests the description need not be a full specification but should be enabling (i.e., sufficient to direct one skilled in the art to make/do the invention). The precise boundaries (what constitutes public work/printed publication) remain to be judicially determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty must cover every material part claimed (entirety rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The consideration for granting a patent is the novelty of every material thing, process, or part included in the subject-matter represented as a substantial and material part; if any part fails, the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent novelty is treated as an entirety: failure of a substantial part (e.g., part of the claim lacks novelty) can invalidate the whole patent. The statute recognizes as a defense that the patentee was not the original and first inventor of a substantial and material part of the thing patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and operability: patent must produce described effect
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent contains more than is necessary to produce the described effect and the addition was made to deceive the public, it will be invalid; if the whole patent fails to produce the described effect, no action can be maintained on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility doctrine: patents must be operable and truthful in description. Overclaiming or adding nonfunctional material to mislead is an invalidating defect. Remedies and defenses (renewal or other proceedings) are discussed elsewhere in the treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject-matter: new and useful art/machine/manufacture/composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent may be granted for any new and useful art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerative statutory standard frames which categories qualify as patentable subjects; later discussion refines these categories with judicial interpretation (e.g., manufacture may include processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture/process must produce an effect in manufactured matter (no abstract principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the subject or its description, the result must be an effect produced in manufactured (corporeal) matter; a mere elementary principle or abstract discovery without practical application is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental rule: patents are not for abstract principles or elementary truths. A principle only becomes patentable when embodied or applied in a practical process, method, machine, or manufacture producing a tangible effect. Examples: Watt's steam conservation method — a principle brought into practical process — was patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject can be a thing produced or a mode of producing it
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter may be either a thing produced (a tangible article) or the mode/process of producing a thing; but it must be one or the other and not merely an effect or abstract principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat 'manufacture' both literally (a new tangible article) and figuratively (a new method/process producing an effect). Patents for new compositions or new processes producing known substances can be proper; but the patent must accurately represent what is claimed (must not claim one thing in the patent and show another in the specification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes/methods are patentable only when they embody/practically apply a principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A process, method, or practical application of a principle may be the subject of a patent provided the patentee has not only discovered the principle but has invented some mode of carrying it into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases sustaining patents for applying gas flame to lace, combining anthracite with hot air blast, or welding tubes without a mandril illustrate that applying a principle by an invented practical mode can be patentable. The mode or apparatus enabling the application is often covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation to prevent monopolization of abstract principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents must be confined to specific applications of principles or methods; allowing patents for abstract arts or universal principles would permit monopolization of fields and exclude others from using the underlying scientific elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise warns against patents that cover abstract arts/principles without confinement to particular products or results. Example: a hypothetical patent on the abstract principle of intermixing water with oil colors would improperly preclude many distinct manufactures; hence patents must be limited to particular modes, products, or practical applications.
